items.title: Companies Act 2006, section 172: Duty to promote the success of the company
items.quote: the interests of the company's employees
items.why: Source of the quotation. Employees' interests are one of six matters directors must have regard to while promoting the company's success for the benefit of its members; the duty is owed to the company, not to employees, and does not prescribe an assessment or a record.

items.title: Companies Act 2006, section 414CZA: Section 172(1) statement
items.quote: describes how the directors have had regard to the matters set out in section 172(1)(a) to (f) when performing their duty under section 172
items.why: The reporting duty that makes the record matter: the strategic report must describe how directors had regard to the section 172 matters. It does not apply to a company that qualifies as medium-sized (and small companies do not prepare a strategic report). Inserted by the Companies (Miscellaneous Reporting) Regulations 2018 (S.I. 2018/860), per the textual note on the page.

items.title: Companies Act 2006, section 248: Minutes of directors' meetings
items.quote: Every company must cause minutes of all proceedings at meetings of its directors to be recorded.
items.why: The duty to minute. It requires a record of proceedings; it does not say what the minute must contain, so a record of the workforce assessment is good practice built on this duty, not a statutory requirement.

items.title: UK Corporate Governance Code 2024
items.quote: have been considered in board discussions and decision-making
items.why: Provision 5 asks the board to describe in the annual report how stakeholder views and the section 172 matters were considered in board discussions and decision-making, and to engage the workforce through a workforce director, an advisory panel or a designated non-executive. Applies on a comply-or-explain basis to listed companies; used by others as a benchmark.

items.title: Trade Union and Labour Relations (Consolidation) Act 1992, section 188: Duty of employer to consult representatives
items.quote: The consultation shall begin in good time and in any event
items.why: The point at which a job-loss effect becomes a legal duty: collective consultation where 20 or more redundancies are proposed at one establishment within 90 days, with written disclosure of reasons and numbers. The page shows prospective amendments from the Employment Rights Act 2025 (a threshold across establishments) in brackets; whether they are in force was not established.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 35: Data protection impact assessment
items.quote: the controller shall seek the views of data subjects or their representatives on the intended processing
items.why: The nearest existing statutory assessment made before adoption: where workplace AI processes staff data at high risk, the assessment comes first and staff or their representatives are asked for their views where appropriate. It covers data protection risk, not job change.

items.title: 1 in 4 workers worry that AI will lead to job losses
items.locator: 'Some top tips for employers from Acas on the use of AI at work'
items.quote: If there is an expectation that certain roles begin using AI, that could mean a change of terms and conditions.
items.why: Acas advice that employers should have clear policies and consult employees and representatives on introducing AI, issued with a survey of 1,023 employees. Advice in a news release, not a statutory code.

items.title: Labour Market Outlook: Autumn 2025
items.locator: Key points (page 5) and section on artificial intelligence (page 16 onwards)
items.quote: Employees in three-quarters of UK organisations are using AI tools at work (76%).
items.why: Source of the figure: 17% of employers expect the use of AI tools to reduce their headcount in the next 12 months; survey of 2,019 UK employers by YouGov, fieldwork 19 September to 14 October 2025. The CIPD's press release says the 17% excludes employers who do not know whether AI tools are used (6% of the sample). Expectations, not outcomes.

items.title: Generative AI and Jobs: A Refined Global Index of Occupational Exposure (ILO Working Paper 140)
items.quote: Globally, one in four workers are in an occupation with some GenAI exposure.
items.why: International comparator. Finds that transformation of jobs, not replacement, is the most likely effect, that exposure is higher for women and in high-income countries, and that the change should be managed through social dialogue. Exposure is a measure of tasks, not a forecast of job losses. No publication date is printed on the web edition; 2025 is taken from the text.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 26: Obligations of deployers of high-risk AI systems
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: deployers who are employers shall inform workers’ representatives and the affected workers that they will be subject to the use of the high-risk AI system
items.why: The Commission's copy, not the Official Journal (EUR-Lex returned an empty page, HTTP 202). A duty to inform before a high-risk system is used at work; it is not a duty to assess job impact. The page carries a notice that the provision was amended by the Digital Omnibus and the text shown is not yet updated; no application date is given in the brief.

items.title: Companies Act 2006, section 170: Scope and nature of general duties
items.quote: The general duties specified in sections 171 to 177 are owed by a director of a company to the company.
items.why: The statutory basis for the brief's statement that the duty is owed to the company, not to staff (the research log recorded this section as not opened). Limits: says to whom the duty is owed, nothing about assessments or records; the page lists pending changes to Schedule 11A only.

items.title: Employment Rights Act 1996, section 139: Redundancy
items.quote: have ceased or diminished or are expected to cease or diminish
items.why: The legal definition that an AI adoption can trigger: a dismissal is by reason of redundancy where the business's need for employees to do work of a particular kind has diminished or is expected to. An assessment that identifies tasks removed is identifying this. Limits: defines redundancy for dismissal and payment purposes; imposes no duty to assess before adopting technology.

items.title: BTI 2014 LLC v Sequana SA and others [2022] UKSC 25
items.publisher: UK Supreme Court, via The National Archives Find Case Law
items.quote: the promotion of the company's success requires that consideration be given to such matters as the interests of its employees
items.why: The Supreme Court's reading of section 172: regard to the listed matters is a 'secondary obligation' within the primary duty to promote the company's success, the duty is owed to the company with shareholders as intended beneficiaries, and good faith is generally judged subjectively. Limits: the case concerned creditors' interests and a dividend, not employees; these passages are general remarks on the section.

items.title: Corporate Governance Code Guidance
items.quote: Ensuring that board minutes document the discussion that led to the decision, including the issues raised and the reasons for the decision.
items.why: The regulator's guidance on recording significant decisions, and the source for expecting stakeholder impact to appear in the minute: paragraph 30 asks whether the board can explain how impact on key stakeholders was taken into account. Limits: not mandatory and not part of the Code; written for companies that apply the Code; page shows last updated 3 June 2026.

items.title: HSE's regulatory approach to artificial intelligence (AI)
items.locator: Policy statement, 'Assess and manage risks from AI in the workplace'
items.quote: Health and safety legislation requires a risk assessment to be undertaken for uses of AI which impact on workplace health and safety
items.why: A regulator stating that an existing statutory assessment already applies to workplace AI: where a use of AI affects health and safety at work, a risk assessment and controls are required. One part of the effect on workers that must be assessed by law. Limits: health and safety only, not jobs, pay or redundancy; a policy statement, with fuller guidance not yet published; Great Britain.

items.title: Use of artificial intelligence in government (HC 612, Session 2023-24)
items.locator: Part Three, paragraph 3.8, 'Assessing workforce impacts' (also Summary paragraph 15)
items.quote: Realising the benefits of large-scale adoption of AI will require changes in the roles of civil servants.
items.why: An audit finding on this exact point: the NAO lists assessing workforce impacts among the lessons to get right at the outset and found the implications for workforce composition and skills were not yet considered in detail in the government's adoption strategy. Limits: central government; position as at March 2024.

items.title: Assessment of AI capabilities and the impact on the UK labour market
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology and AI Security Institute
items.locator: Evidence judgement 2 (see also judgement 4 on hiring)
items.quote: Around 70% of UK workers are in occupations containing tasks that AI could potentially perform or enhance, according to IMF estimates.
items.why: The government's own summary of the evidence a board assessment should start from: high exposure in a service economy, and job postings falling faster in more exposed occupations, with cause not established. Limits: a high-level review of others' studies, not new data; the 70% figure is the IMF's exposure measure, not a forecast of job losses.

items.title: Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence
items.publisher: Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen; Stanford Digital Economy Lab working paper
items.locator: Section 1, summary of the six facts (abstract gives the same figure for ages 22-25)
items.quote: young workers experienced a 16% relative employment decline in the most exposed occupations
items.why: Large-scale payroll evidence that effects fall unevenly: entry-level workers in the most exposed occupations lost ground while experienced workers did not, and declines were in uses that automate work, not those that augment it. A reason for an assessment to look at who is affected, not only how many. Limits: working paper, not peer reviewed; US data from one payroll provider; the authors caution that other factors may contribute; the paper is revised from time to time at the same address.

items.title: Good Work Algorithmic Impact Assessment: an approach for worker involvement
items.publisher: Institute for the Future of Work
items.quote: help employers and engineers to involve workers and their representatives in the design, development and deployment of algorithmic systems
items.why: A published UK method for the assessment this criterion asks about, produced with support from the Information Commissioner's Office grants programme: assess effects on access to work, conditions and job quality, with workers involved. Limits: voluntary guidance from a research charity, not a regulator's standard; 2023; the summary page was read, not the full guidance document.

items.title: OECD AI Principles, Principle 2.4: Building human capacity and preparing for labour market transformation
items.publisher: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD.AI)
items.quote: Governments should take steps, including through social dialogue, to ensure a fair transition for workers as AI is deployed
items.why: International comparator: the intergovernmental standard the UK adheres to treats transition for workers, through training, support for those displaced and social dialogue, as part of trustworthy AI. Limits: addressed to governments, not companies; non-binding; the page is undated and the year given is that of the revised Recommendation as generally reported, not a date printed on the page.
